Finasteride

FDA-approved for male pattern hair loss. Lowers DHT, the hormone that shrinks follicles.

Minoxidil

The Manes
formulary

Four ingredients your clinician can draw from. Open one to see what it does, and what to know before you start.

Finasteride

What it does

Blocks 5α-reductase type II, lowering DHT, the hormone that miniaturizes genetically sensitive follicles. FDA-approved for men since 1997.

Worth knowing

Sexual side effects were reported by 3.8% of men vs 2.1% on placebo in trials. Depression and suicidal thoughts are listed as reported reactions. It lowers PSA test results.

What it does

Thought to lengthen the growth phase and enlarge follicles, partly by improving blood flow. Its exact mechanism isn’t fully understood.

Worth knowing

Scalp irritation and temporary early shedding are common. Benefits fade within months of stopping.

What it does

The same active ingredient as the topical, taken as a small daily tablet. A 2025 international expert consensus supports careful off-label use.

Worth knowing

FDA-approved only for high blood pressure. Can cause unwanted body hair, fluid retention or a faster heartbeat, so your clinician screens your heart history first.

What it does

Designed to act mainly on the scalp. Often paired with minoxidil in a single serum.

Worth knowing

Not FDA-approved and less studied than the oral form. Some is absorbed into the body, so similar side effects remain possible.

The honest timeline.
Month by month.

Hair grows slowly, so treatment is measured in months. Here’s the honest version.

Get started

Months 1–3: Treatment gets to work

Effects start below the surface first.

  • Finasteride begins lowering DHT
  • Some temporary shedding is possible with minoxidil
  • Baseline photos set your starting point

Months 4–6: Shedding slows

Often the first change men notice.

  • Many men see less hair in the shower and on the pillow
  • Visible change can begin around month six
  • A photo check-in with your clinician

Months 6–12+: Judge and adjust

The fair point to measure results.

  • Clinicians typically assess response at 6–12 months
  • In trials, gains held through two years of continued use
  • Benefits fade if treatment stops
